title: Stokes’ theorem
objectives: Turn a line integral around a boundary into a surface integral of the curl.

screens.title: Two caps on one circle
screens.prose: The rotation field $\mathbf F = (-y, x, 0)$ has circulation $2\pi$ round the unit circle in $z = 0$, counterclockwise from above. Its curl is $(0, 0, 2)$. Through the flat disc, normal up, the curl's flux is $2 \times \pi = 2\pi$. The upper hemisphere has the same boundary circle.
screens.question: Predict the curl's flux up through the hemisphere.

options.text: $2\pi$, the same as the disc
Less than $2\pi$, since the hemisphere's normals tilt away from $(0, 0, 2)$
options.why: Tilted normals catch less per unit area, but the hemisphere has twice the area.

options.text: $4\pi$, since the hemisphere has twice the disc's area
options.why: You multiplied $|\nabla \times \mathbf F|$ by the area. The normals tilt, so each patch catches less.

hints.text: Both surfaces have the same boundary, $C$.
Lesson 6 linked circulation and curl through the disc.

feedback.correct: The hemisphere also gives $2\pi$; we check it next.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the two surfaces share.

byKey.less: The tilt and the extra area cancel exactly.
byKey.more: Flux uses $\mathbf n$, which tilts away from $(0, 0, 2)$.

explain.text: The two surfaces share the boundary $C$, and both fluxes equal the circulation $2\pi$. Tilt loses flux per patch and extra area gains it back.

screens.title: Check on the hemisphere
screens.prose: On the unit sphere $\mathbf r_\phi \times \mathbf r_\theta = \sin\phi\,(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\ \sin\phi\sin\theta,\ \cos\phi)$. Dotted with the curl $(0, 0, 2)$ it gives $2\cos\phi\sin\phi$.
screens.question: What is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2} 2\cos\phi\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Do the $\phi$ integral first.

byKey.area: $4\pi$ is $|\nabla \times \mathbf F|$ times the hemisphere's area. The dot product brings in $\cos\phi$.
byKey.half: You lost the factor 2 from the curl.

explain.text: $\int_0^{\pi/2} 2\cos\phi\sin\phi\,d\phi = 1$, so the flux is $2\pi$. The disc, the hemisphere and the circulation all agree.

screens.title: Which way round
screens.prose:
This is **Stokes' theorem**: $$\oint_C \mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf F) \cdot \mathbf n\,dS$$
It holds for an orientable piecewise smooth surface $S$ with boundary curve $C$, and $\mathbf F$ continuously differentiable on $S$. The orientations must match by the **right-hand rule**: thumb along $\mathbf n$, fingers along $C$.
screens.question: With $\mathbf n$ pointing out of this hemisphere, which way must $C$ run?

options.text: Counterclockwise seen from above
Clockwise seen from above
options.why: That pairs with the inward normal. With the thumb up, the fingers curl counterclockwise from above.

options.text: Either way; Stokes does not care
options.why: Reversing $C$ flips the left side's sign but not the right side's. They must be matched.

options.text: Along $\mathbf n$, straight up
options.why: $C$ lies in the plane $z = 0$; it runs round, not along the normal.

hints.text: Point your right thumb up the normal at the top.
Seen from above, that is counterclockwise.

feedback.correct: Outward normal on the dome, counterclockwise boundary from above.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use your right hand: thumb along $\mathbf n$.

byKey.cw: Clockwise goes with $\mathbf n$ pointing into the dome.
byKey.either: Each side has a sign; the right-hand rule ties them together.
byKey.along: The boundary is a curve round the rim.

explain.text: Thumb along the outward normal, fingers curl counterclockwise seen from above. That is the orientation we used for $2\pi$ on both caps.

screens.title: Curl as a cross product
screens.prose:
Write $\nabla = (\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)$ and cross it with $\mathbf F = (P, Q, R)$ by the formula of lesson 9: $$\nabla \times \mathbf F = (R_y - Q_z,\ P_z - R_x,\ Q_x - P_y).$$
These are the components of lesson 5. Take $\mathbf F = (z, x, y)$.
screens.question: What is $\nabla \times \mathbf F$? Give $(a, b, c)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each entry as a difference of two partials.

byKey.sign: Each entry is in a fixed order: $R_y - Q_z$, not $Q_z - R_y$.
byKey.div: You took $P_x$, $Q_y$, $R_z$, the parts of the divergence. The curl uses mixed partials.

explain.text: $R_y = 1$, $P_z = 1$ and $Q_x = 1$, and the other three partials are 0. So $\nabla \times \mathbf F = (1, 1, 1)$, constant.

screens.title: Why the surface does not matter
screens.prose: Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be orientable surfaces with the same boundary $C$. Both are oriented to match $C$ by the right-hand rule, and together they enclose a solid $E$. Let $\mathbf F$ be twice continuously differentiable on $E$.
screens.question: Put the derivation in order. Leave out the flawed line.

lines.text: $S_1$ and $S_2$ together form the closed boundary of $E$. (They share $C$.)

The outward flux of $
abla 	imes \mathbf F$ through it is $\iiint_E 
abla \cdot (
abla 	imes \mathbf F)\,dV$. (Divergence theorem.)
$\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf F) = 0$: the mixed partials cancel in pairs. (Clairaut.)
Outward is the chosen normal on $S_1$ and its reverse on $S_2$. So flux through $S_1$ minus flux through $S_2$ is 0. (Orientation.)
Outward is the chosen normal on both, so the two fluxes add to 0. (Orientation.)
lines.why: Two caps on one circle, both oriented by $C$, point the same way across it. So one points into $E$.

hints.text: Glue the two surfaces into one closed surface.
Apply the divergence theorem to $\nabla \times \mathbf F$.
The divergence of a curl is 0.

feedback.correct: Every surface on $C$ carries the same flux of the curl.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Close the surface, use the divergence theorem, then mind the normals.

byKey.d1: With both oriented by $C$, one normal points into $E$. The fluxes are equal, not opposite.
byKey.left-out: All five true lines are needed.

explain.text: The two caps bound a solid, and the curl has divergence 0, so its net outward flux is 0. One cap's outward normal is its chosen normal and the other's is reversed. So the two chosen fluxes are equal, as the disc and hemisphere showed.

screens.title: Round the circle
screens.prose: Now $\mathbf F = (z, x, y)$ round the unit circle $\mathbf r(t) = (\cos t, \sin t, 0)$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$. On it $\mathbf F = (0, \cos t, \sin t)$ and $\mathbf r' = (-\sin t, \cos t, 0)$, so the integrand is $\cos^2 t$.
screens.question: What is the circulation $\oint_C \mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r$?

feedback.correct: $\int_0^{2\pi} \cos^2 t\,dt = \pi$. By Stokes on the disc, $(1, 1, 1) \cdot (0, 0, 1) = 1$ times area $\pi$ agrees.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $\cos^2 t$ over a full turn.

byKey.full: You integrated 1, not $\cos^2 t$. Its average is $\tfrac12$.
byKey.zero: $\cos^2 t$ is never negative, so the integral is positive.

explain.text: $\int_0^{2\pi} \cos^2 t\,dt = \pi$. Through the disc with $\mathbf n = (0, 0, 1)$, $(\nabla \times \mathbf F) \cdot \mathbf n = 1$, over area $\pi$: also $\pi$.

screens.title: Round a triangle
screens.prose: Take the same field round the triangle with corners $(1, 0, 0)$, $(0, 1, 0)$, $(0, 0, 1)$, in that order. Seen from above it runs counterclockwise. Each edge is $\mathbf r(t) = \mathbf A + t(\mathbf B - \mathbf A)$, $0 \le t \le 1$.
screens.question: Fill in each edge's work and the total.

hints.text: First edge: $\mathbf r = (1 - t, t, 0)$, $\mathbf F = (0, 1 - t, t)$, $\mathbf r' = (-1, 1, 0)$.
The other two edges give the same by symmetry.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Parametrise each edge and integrate $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf r'$.

byKey.one: You integrated 1 instead of $1 - t$. The integrand falls to 0 along each edge.

explain.text: On each edge $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf r' = 1 - t$, which integrates to $\tfrac12$. The three edges give $\tfrac32$. The field and the triangle both keep their shape when $x \to y \to z \to x$, which is why the edges agree.

screens.title: The triangle by Stokes
screens.prose: The flat triangle lies on $z = 1 - x - y$ over the shadow $x, y \ge 0$, $x + y \le 1$. Its upward $\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y = (1, 1, 1)$, matching the counterclockwise boundary by the right-hand rule. The curl is $(1, 1, 1)$.
screens.question: What is $\iint (\nabla \times \mathbf F) \cdot \mathbf n\,dS$, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot the curl with $(1, 1, 1)$ and integrate over the shadow.

byKey.unit-n: You used the unit normal with $dA$ instead of $dS$. Either take $(1, 1, 1)\,dA$ or $\tfrac{(1, 1, 1)}{\sqrt3}\,dS$.
byKey.no-shadow: You integrated over a unit square. The shadow is half of it.

explain.text: $(\nabla \times \mathbf F) \cdot (1, 1, 1) = 3$ over a shadow of area $\tfrac12$ gives $\tfrac32$. The three edges gave $\tfrac32$ too.

screens.title: Swap a hard surface for an easy one
screens.prose: Take $\mathbf F = (-y,\ x,\ z^2e^x)$. Its curl is $(0,\ -z^2e^x,\ 2)$, awkward to integrate over the cap $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2$, $z \ge 0$, normal up. The cap's boundary is the unit circle in $z = 0$, counterclockwise from above.
screens.question: What is the flux of $\nabla \times \mathbf F$ up through the cap?

hints.text: By Stokes it is the circulation round the unit circle.

feedback.correct: The circulation round the circle is $2\pi$, so the flux is $2\pi$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use Stokes and work round the circle instead.

byKey.area: $\pi$ is the shadow's area. The curl's $z$ entry is 2.

explain.text: Stokes trades the cap for its boundary. On the circle $z = 0$ and $dz = 0$, so $\oint -y\,dx + x\,dy = 2\pi$. The cap's flux is $2\pi$ without touching $e^x$.

screens.title: Mismatched orientation
screens.prose: A classmate takes $\mathbf F = (z, x, y)$ through the disc with $\mathbf n$ up, and computes the circulation with $C$ clockwise seen from above. They get $-\pi$ and call Stokes wrong.
screens.question: What went wrong?

options.text: The boundary runs against the right-hand rule; counterclockwise gives $\pi$, matching the flux
Nothing: Stokes gives $-\pi$ here
options.why: You kept the clockwise boundary. With $\mathbf n$ up the right-hand rule needs counterclockwise, which gives $\pi$.

options.text: Stokes needs a curved surface, not a flat disc
options.why: Any orientable piecewise smooth surface works; the flat disc is Green's case.

hints.text: Point your thumb up the normal.
Your fingers curl counterclockwise from above.

feedback.correct: Match $C$ to $\mathbf n$ by the right-hand rule, and both sides give $\pi$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the boundary's direction against the normal.

byKey.negpi: The theorem holds only with matched orientations. Clockwise pairs with $\mathbf n$ down.
byKey.flat: Flat surfaces are allowed. Stokes on a flat region is Green's theorem.

explain.text: Clockwise round $C$ gives $-\pi$, the reverse of counterclockwise. With $\mathbf n$ up, the right-hand rule wants counterclockwise. Then both sides give $\pi$.

screens.title: No boundary at all
screens.prose: The unit sphere is a closed surface: it has no boundary curve. Take the curl of $(-y,\ x,\ z^2e^x)$ again, and the outward normal.
screens.question: What is the outward flux of $\nabla \times \mathbf F$ through the sphere?

options.text: $4\pi$, twice the hemisphere's $2\pi$
options.why: You added the two hemispheres with the same orientation. Outward on the lower half is the reverse, so they cancel.

options.text: Stokes cannot say, since there is no boundary
options.why: With no boundary the circulation side is 0. The divergence theorem agrees: $\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf F) = 0$.

hints.text: Cut the sphere at the equator.
Each half has the equator as boundary, run in opposite directions for outward normals.

feedback.correct: The flux of a curl out of a closed surface is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the sphere into two hemispheres and compare their boundaries.

byKey.fourpi: Outward on the bottom half points down: its boundary runs clockwise from above, giving $-2\pi$.
byKey.cannot: No boundary means zero circulation, so zero flux.

explain.text: Cut at the equator. Outward normals make the two boundaries run opposite ways, so the fluxes $2\pi$ and $-2\pi$ cancel to 0. Lesson 11 agrees: $\iiint \nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf F)\,dV = 0$ for $\mathbf F$ twice continuously differentiable.

screens.title: A loop in three prices
screens.prose: A strategy holds $\mathbf h = (0,\ S_1 - 100,\ 0)$ shares of three stocks, so its P&L is $\int \mathbf h \cdot d\mathbf S$. Its curl is $(0, 0, 1)$. Prices start at £100 each and trace the loop drawn. First $S_1$ rises, then $S_2$ and $S_3$; then $S_1$ falls back, then $S_2$ and $S_3$.
screens.question: Fill in the P&L on each leg and the total, in £.

hints.text: On leg 2 the strategy holds 10 shares of stock 2.

feedback.correct: £0, £50, £0, £0: £50, the area of the loop's shadow on the $(S_1, S_2)$ plane.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each leg's $S_2$ move by $S_1 - 100$ on that leg.

byKey.held-old: On leg 2 $S_1$ is already 110, so the strategy holds 10 shares.
byKey.wrong-leg: Leg 3 moves only $S_1$, and the holding in stock 1 is 0.
byKey.held-new: On leg 4 $S_1$ is back at 100, so the holding is 0.

explain.text: Only leg 2 earns: 10 shares times a £5 rise is £50. By Stokes, a curl of $(0, 0, 1)$ makes the P&L the area of the loop's shadow on the $(S_1, S_2)$ plane, $10 \times 5 = 50$. The move in $S_3$ adds nothing.

ideas: Let $S$ be orientable and piecewise smooth, with boundary $C$ oriented by the right-hand rule. For $\mathbf F$ continuously differentiable on $S$, $\oint_C \mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf F) \cdot \mathbf n\,dS$.
Two such surfaces on the same $C$ carry the same flux of the curl, since $\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf F) = 0$; pick the easier one.
A flat region in the plane gives Green's theorem. A closed surface has no boundary, so a curl's flux out of it is 0.

formula.name: Stokes' theorem
formula.note: Thumb along n, fingers along C.

summary.trap: A clockwise boundary with an upward normal flips the sign: $-\pi$ instead of $\pi$ for $(z, x, y)$.

quiz.prose: Take a flat region $D$ in the plane $z = 0$ with $\mathbf n = (0, 0, 1)$ and $\mathbf F = (P, Q, 0)$.
quiz.question: What does $(\nabla \times \mathbf F) \cdot \mathbf n$ become?

options.text: $Q_x - P_y$, so Stokes becomes Green's theorem
$P_x + Q_y$
options.why: That is the divergence. The $z$ entry of the curl is $Q_x - P_y$.

options.text: 0, since $R = 0$
options.why: Only the $x$ and $y$ entries of the curl vanish here.

feedback.correct: Stokes on a flat region is Green.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the $z$ entry of the curl.

byKey.div: Divergence belongs to the flux form.

explain.text: The $z$ entry of $\nabla \times \mathbf F$ is $Q_x - P_y$, and $dS = dA$. So $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y)\,dA$: Green's theorem.

quiz.question: Why does the $z^2e^x$ part of $(-y, x, z^2e^x)$ add nothing round the unit circle in $z = 0$?

options.text: It multiplies $dz$, and $dz = 0$ on a curve in the plane $z = 0$
Its curl is 0
options.why: Its curl is $(0, -z^2e^x, 0)$, not 0. It drops out because of where the curve lies.

options.text: $e^x$ is odd round the circle

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what $R$ multiplies in $\mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r$.

explain.text: $\mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r = P\,dx + Q\,dy + R\,dz$, and $dz = 0$ when $z$ is constant. Also $z = 0$ there, so $R = 0$ on the circle.

quiz.question: When is a strategy's P&L zero round every closed price loop?

options.text: When its holdings field has zero curl on a region with no holes, so it is a gradient
Only when the holdings are constant
options.why: Any gradient field works, such as $\mathbf h = \nabla f$ for a smooth $f$.

options.text: Whenever the curl is zero, on any region
options.why: On a region with a hole, zero curl can still allow a loop with non-zero P&L. The vortex showed this.

feedback.correct: Zero curl on a region with no holes means a potential, and path-independent P&L.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall when a field is a gradient.

byKey.const: Constant holdings are one example of a gradient, not the only one.
byKey.curl-only: The region must have no holes.

explain.text: By Stokes, each loop's P&L is the flux of the curl through a surface spanning it. On a region with no holes every loop has such a surface, so zero curl gives zero P&L. That is lesson 4's potential again.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf F = (z, x, y)$ has curl $(1, 1, 1)$. Take the disc $x^2 + y^2 \le 4$ in $z = 0$, normal up.
quiz.question: What is the circulation round its counterclockwise boundary, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot the curl with the normal and multiply by the area.

byKey.unit: That is the unit disc. This disc has radius 2.
byKey.three: You used $|\nabla \times \mathbf F|^2 = 3$. Only the $z$ entry crosses the disc.

explain.text: Only the $z$ entry, 1, crosses the disc. The area is $4\pi$, so the circulation is $4\pi \approx 12.566$.
